newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico says $1.2 bln refinery expansion approved.
newsitem.headline: Mexico says $1.2 bln refinery expansion approved.

text.p: State oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) said Wednesday that it had received approval for a $1.2 billion expansion of its Cadereyta refinery in the northern state of Nuevo Leon and would publish an international invitation to bid for the work September 5.

"The total investment in this project is estimated at almost $1.2 billion and has been authorised as 'financed public work'," Pemex said in a statement. "This means that all the work required for the Cadereyta project will be carried out with financial resources provided by the general contract-holder who wins the respective international public tender."
"When the construction period is over and the work has been received, payments made by Pemex under this financing scheme will come from the flow of resources generated by the project itself."
Pemex said the project consisted of the construction of 10 new plants and the modernisation of another six, together with related secondary work.

The expansion was aimed at producing cleaner fuels with lower sulphur content, reducing output of high-sulphur fuel oil, meeting growing regional demand for gasoline and diesel fuel, processing more heavy crude and stepping up the refinery's output to 270,000 bpd of crude from 235,000.

Pemex, which made the announcements after a board meeting held Wednesday, also said it plans to boost the output of its Cantarell oil field in the Bay of Campeche by 150,000 bpd in 1997 from 1.1 million bpd now.

The plan, entailing investment of $825 million in 1997, would also end the release of natural gas into the atmosphere in the Bay of Campeche, increase operational flexibility in the Cantarell field and develop a pressure-maintenance programme for the fields, injecting natural gas and later other gases, Pemex said.
It said U.S. firm Bechtel would provide techical assistance to Pemex in the administration of the project.
Pemex also confirmed that as of Wednesday it was no longer importing natural gas as a result of the explosion in July at its Cactus gas-processing plant in the southern state of Chiapas.
It said natural gas processing was down nine percent compared to before the blast but that it expected to reduce that figure to two percent by the end of the year.
Natural gas output was down six percent compared to before the explosion, Pemex said.

"Pemex has also been obliged to liberate into the atmosphere a volume of gas equal to less than one percent of current output of associated gas," Pemex said, adding the burning was done at sea to limit environmental effects.
